triage.name: Cataract
triage.reason: Progressive painless vision loss with an abnormal red reflex and slit-lamp findings; straightforward clinic presentation, though exam findings are specialty-specific.

review_issues: auto-repaired: workup: 'slit-lamp examination of the anterior segment' was in ['initial', 'confirmatory'], kept ['initial']
presentation: older format without SNOMED terms
exam: older format without SNOMED terms

demographics: Very common with advancing age; by age 80 more than half of Americans have a cataract or have had cataract surgery
Slightly more common in women in most US surveys
More prevalent and more likely to cause vision loss in Black and Hispanic adults in the US

risk_factors.text: Cumulative ultraviolet light exposure (sun, tanning, welding)
Prior eye injury or prior eye surgery (e.g., glaucoma surgery)

family_history: Cataract in a parent or sibling, especially early-onset
social_history: Outdoor work or long hours in the sun without eye protection
exposures: Ionizing radiation to the head or neck

chief_complaints.text: My vision has gotten blurry and cloudy
The headlights at night are blinding and there are halos around lights
I keep needing new glasses prescriptions
Colors don't look as bright as they used to
I can't see well enough to read or drive anymore

hpi.onset: Gradual and painless, usually noticed only after it has been present for months
hpi.duration: Months to years; most patients have had subtle changes for a year or more before seeking care
hpi.progression: Slowly progressive and irreversible; vision worsens as the lens opacity thickens, and symptoms eventually interfere with reading, driving, or recognizing faces
hpi.location: One or both eyes; when unilateral, the affected eye is the symptomatic one
hpi.quality: Blurring, cloudiness, or a film over the vision; glare and halos around lights; washed-out or yellowed color perception
hpi.severity: Mild at first and often dismissed as needing new glasses; becomes moderate to severe when it limits daily activities
hpi.timing: Constant, but worse in dim light, at night, and with bright oncoming lights; some patients notice better near vision than distance vision (second sight)

associated_symptoms.text: Glare from headlights, lamps, or sunlight
Double vision in one eye that goes away when the other eye is covered
Frequent changes in glasses or contact lens prescription
Trouble reading or doing everyday tasks

pertinent_negatives: Sudden vision loss over minutes to hours
Flashes of light or a curtain/shade across the vision
Severe headache with nausea and vomiting

atypical.how_it_differs: Pediatric cataracts are usually congenital or associated with a syndrome, metabolic disease, or intrauterine infection; infants may present with a white pupil (leukocoria), poor visual tracking, or strabismus rather than complaints of blurry vision.
missing_classic_features: Glare and halos described by the patient

atypical.how_it_differs: Cataracts appear earlier and progress faster, and fluctuating blood glucose can cause rapid but reversible refractive shifts that mimic cataract progression.
missing_classic_features: Clear temporal link to aging alone

atypical.how_it_differs: Patients may not report vision problems at all; instead they present with falls, difficulty reading medication labels, or a family member noticing they can no longer drive safely.

general.mild: Comfortable, well-appearing, no distress; may squint or lean toward the examiner
general.moderate: Well-appearing but visibly straining to read or recognize faces; may hold materials at arm's length
general.severe: Well-appearing but functionally limited; may need help navigating the room or reading forms
general.critical: Not applicable; cataract alone does not cause a toxic or systemically ill appearance

findings.maneuver: Check distance visual acuity one eye at a time with a Snellen chart, with the patient's current glasses on
findings.finding: Reduced best-corrected distance acuity in the affected eye(s)

findings.maneuver: Repeat the acuity measurement through a pinhole occluder
findings.finding: Acuity improves only partially or not at all, unlike a pure refractive error

findings.maneuver: Shine the ophthalmoscope light into the eye from about 12 inches and observe the red reflex
findings.finding: Dull, diminished, or absent red reflex; may see dark opacities within the reflex

findings.maneuver: Examine the anterior segment at the slit lamp after pupil dilation
findings.finding: Visible lens opacity (nuclear sclerosis, cortical spokes, or posterior subcapsular plaque)

findings.maneuver: Shine a bright light or penlight toward the eye and ask about discomfort or worsening of vision
findings.finding: Marked glare or worsening of vision with bright light

findings.maneuver: Check pupil size, symmetry, and reactivity to light
findings.finding: Pupils equal, round, and reactive; no afferent pupillary defect

findings.maneuver: Inspect the pupil in room light and with the ophthalmoscope
Inspect the conjunctiva and sclera in room light
findings.finding: White sclera with no injection, discharge, or ciliary flush

findings.maneuver: Palpate gently around the orbit and ask about eye pain
Measure intraocular pressure by tonometry when available
findings.finding: Intraocular pressure within the normal range
Optic disc, macula, and vessels appear normal; no hemorrhages, exudates, or disc edema

findings.maneuver: Test extraocular movements in all directions of gaze
findings.finding: Full, conjugate, and painless eye movements without diplopia

findings.maneuver: Confrontation visual fields in each eye
findings.finding: Full visual fields without scotoma or field cut

findings.maneuver: Screen cranial nerves, strength, sensation, and coordination

imaging.study: Slit-lamp examination of the anterior segment

findings.text: Lens opacity: nuclear sclerosis (yellow-brown central haze), cortical spokes, or posterior subcapsular plaque
Dense white or brunescent lens opacity obscuring the red reflex
Normal anterior chamber, cornea, and iris without cells or flare
Optic disc, macula, and vessels normal; no hemorrhages, exudates, or disc edema
Lens opacity partially obscures the view of the posterior pole
Incidental diabetic or hypertensive retinopathy in a patient with those comorbidities

imaging.study: Optical coherence tomography of the macula
imaging.preferred_when: Suspected coexisting macular disease before cataract surgery

findings.text: Normal macular architecture with intact foveal contour
Macular edema, epiretinal membrane, or drusen suggesting a coexisting retinal condition

imaging.preferred_when: Dense cataract prevents a view of the posterior segment

findings.text: Normal posterior segment with no retinal detachment or mass
Retinal detachment or intraocular mass identified behind the opaque lens

initial.why: Establishes the degree of vision loss and whether it improves with correction

initial.test: Slit-lamp examination of the anterior segment
initial.why: Directly visualizes the lens opacity and classifies its type
Evaluates the retina and optic nerve for coexisting disease
Bedside screen for lens opacity and leukocoria

supporting.test: Optical coherence tomography of the macula
supporting.why: Detects macular disease that could limit visual recovery after surgery
supporting.only_if: macular pathology is suspected or the fundus view is poor

supporting.why: Assesses the posterior segment when the lens is too opaque to see through
Identifies diabetes, which accelerates cataract formation and affects surgical planning
supporting.only_if: diabetes is suspected or glycemic control is unknown

supporting.why: Screens for hyperglycemia that can cause reversible refractive fluctuation
supporting.only_if: the patient reports rapid changes in glasses prescription

not_indicated.why: No role in an isolated lens opacity
Not needed for diagnosis; obtain only for preoperative clearance when indicated
Does not help diagnose cataract; consider only if giant cell arteritis is suspected
Not part of the cataract workup unless thyroid eye disease is suspected

not_indicated.test: MRI of the brain and orbits
not_indicated.why: Not indicated for a lens opacity; reserved for suspected intracranial or orbital pathology

decision_points: Cataract surgery is offered when the opacity limits the patient's daily activities, not based on acuity alone
Dilated fundus examination and macular assessment before surgery to identify coexisting retinal disease
In infants and children with leukocoria, evaluate urgently for retinoblastoma and congenital cataract

differential.name: Open-angle glaucoma
differential.why_considered: Both are common causes of progressive, painless vision loss in older adults and frequently coexist.
differential.trigger: Peripheral vision loss, elevated intraocular pressure, or optic disc cupping

history: Gradual loss of peripheral vision rather than central blurring
exam: Optic disc cupping with increased cup-to-disc ratio
imaging: Optical coherence tomography showing retinal nerve fiber layer thinning

differential.name: Age-related macular degeneration
differential.why_considered: Common cause of central vision loss in older adults that can be mistaken for cataract.
differential.trigger: Central vision distortion or scotoma with relatively preserved peripheral vision

exam: Reduced central acuity with normal peripheral fields
Drusen, pigmentary changes, or macular hemorrhage on fundoscopy
imaging: Optical coherence tomography showing drusen, subretinal fluid, or macular thickening

differential.name: Diabetic retinopathy
differential.why_considered: Diabetes is a strong risk factor for cataract, and diabetic retinopathy can cause similar visual symptoms.
differential.trigger: Known diabetes with floaters, fluctuating vision, or retinal findings

exam: Microaneurysms, hemorrhages, exudates, or neovascularization on fundoscopy
imaging: Fluorescein angiography showing leakage or ischemia
Optical coherence tomography showing macular edema

differential.name: Retinal detachment
differential.why_considered: Can present with sudden visual changes that patients may attribute to cataract.
differential.trigger: Sudden onset of flashes, floaters, or a curtain-like visual field defect

history: Sudden onset of flashes and floaters
exam: Retinal tear or detachment on dilated fundoscopy
imaging: Ocular ultrasound showing retinal detachment if fundus view is obscured

differential.name: Primary open-angle glaucoma suspect
differential.why_considered: Patients with risk factors for glaucoma may have subtle visual complaints overlapping with cataract.

exam: Suspicious optic disc appearance without definite field loss
imaging: Optical coherence tomography showing borderline nerve fiber layer thinning

differential.name: Uveitis
differential.why_considered: Can cause blurred vision and is associated with cataract formation, especially in younger patients.

exam: Ciliary flush, cells and flare in the anterior chamber
labs: Elevated inflammatory markers if systemic disease suspected

severity.mild: Early lens opacity; vision still adequate for most activities, occasional glare or need for brighter light, and symptoms may be managed with new glasses.
severity.moderate: Increasing opacity; noticeable blurring, glare, halos, and difficulty with night driving or reading small print; interferes with some daily activities.
severity.severe: Dense opacity; vision significantly impaired, limiting reading, driving, and recognizing faces; surgery is typically indicated.
severity.critical: Not applicable; cataract alone is not life-threatening.

red_flags.meaning: Suggests retinal artery occlusion, vitreous hemorrhage, or retinal detachment rather than cataract
Suggests uveitis, acute angle-closure glaucoma, or keratitis

red_flags.finding: Flashes of light or new floaters

red_flags.meaning: Requires urgent evaluation for retinoblastoma or congenital cataract

complications.name: Posterior capsular opacification
clues: Gradual return of blurry vision months to years after cataract surgery
Cloudy posterior capsule on slit-lamp exam

complications.name: Endophthalmitis
clues: Severe eye pain, redness, and vision loss days after surgery

complications.name: Retinal detachment
clues: Sudden flashes, floaters, or visual field defect after surgery

special_populations.differences: Pediatric cataracts are often congenital or associated with syndromes, metabolic disorders, or intrauterine infections; they may present with leukocoria, strabismus, or poor visual tracking and require urgent evaluation to prevent amblyopia.
May not report vision problems; instead present with falls, difficulty reading medication labels, or family noticing unsafe driving.
Cataracts appear earlier and progress faster; fluctuating blood glucose can cause reversible refractive changes that mimic cataract progression.

key_questions.question: How has your vision changed, and how long has this been going on?
key_questions.looking_for: Gradual, painless blurring or cloudiness over months to years

key_questions.question: Is the change in one eye or both?
key_questions.looking_for: One or both eyes; cataract does not spread between eyes

key_questions.question: What makes your vision worse?
key_questions.looking_for: Dim light, night driving, bright lights and oncoming headlights

key_questions.question: Do you see glare or halos around lights?
key_questions.looking_for: Glare and halos, especially at night

key_questions.question: Have your glasses or contact lens prescriptions been changing often?
key_questions.looking_for: Frequent prescription changes; may report better near vision than before

key_questions.question: Do colors look faded or yellowed?
Do you see double? Does it go away when you cover one eye?
key_questions.looking_for: Monocular double vision that resolves with one eye covered

key_questions.question: Is there any eye pain, redness, or discharge?
key_questions.looking_for: Absent; pain or redness points to uveitis, acute angle-closure glaucoma, or keratitis

key_questions.question: Did the vision loss come on suddenly, or have you had flashes, new floaters, or a curtain across your vision?
key_questions.looking_for: Absent; these suggest retinal detachment or vascular occlusion

key_questions.question: Does this interfere with reading, driving, watching TV, or recognizing faces?
key_questions.looking_for: Functional limitation; this is what drives the decision to offer surgery

key_questions.question: Do you have diabetes, or any other health problems?
key_questions.looking_for: Diabetes accelerates cataract formation and affects surgical planning

key_questions.question: Have you ever had an eye injury or eye surgery?
key_questions.looking_for: Prior trauma or surgery (e.g., glaucoma surgery) as a cause

key_questions.question: Do you take steroid medicines, by mouth, injection, or as eye drops?
key_questions.looking_for: Chronic corticosteroid use as a risk factor

key_questions.question: Does anyone in your family have cataracts, especially at a young age?
Do you smoke or drink alcohol?
key_questions.looking_for: Current or past smoking, heavy alcohol use

key_questions.question: Do you spend a lot of time outdoors or in the sun without eye protection?

reasoning_points: Gradual, painless, progressive blurring or cloudiness of vision over months to years
Glare and halos around lights, worse at night and with oncoming headlights
Frequent changes in eyeglass prescription and faded color perception
Reduced best-corrected distance acuity that improves only partially through a pinhole
Dull or diminished red reflex and a visible lens opacity on slit-lamp exam
No eye pain, redness, discharge, or acute red-flag features such as flashes, floaters, or a curtain across the vision
Risk factors such as older age, diabetes, ultraviolet exposure, smoking, steroid use, or prior eye injury or surgery

easy: Older adult with months of gradually worsening, painless blurry vision
Glare and halos with night driving
Reduced acuity that does not correct fully with refraction
Dull red reflex and a visible lens opacity on slit-lamp exam
medium: Patient attributes the change to needing new glasses and reports frequent prescription changes
Monocular double vision or faded color vision as the main complaint
Diabetes with fluctuating vision from both refractive shifts and cataract
Coexisting glaucoma or macular degeneration that must be separated from the cataract
hard: Older adult who does not report vision problems and instead presents with falls or trouble reading medication labels
Dense cataract obscuring the fundus so the posterior segment cannot be assessed
Younger patient with steroid-induced or post-traumatic cataract
Child with leukocoria or poor visual tracking rather than complaints of blurry vision
